3. An ordinance can be used to amend the Constitution if urgent circumstances require it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is incorrect — an ordinance can be issued only when BOTH Houses are not in session OR when EITHER House is not in session (since a law requires both Houses); an ordinance made when both Houses are simultaneously in session is void. Statement 3 is also incorrect — an ordinance CANNOT be used to amend the Constitution under any circumstances. Statement 2 alone is correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the recommendation-and-reconsideration mechanism under Articles 74 and its amendments:
1. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 made the President's action bound by ministerial advice for the first time.
2. The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed this binding requirement altogether, restoring full presidential discretion.
3. The 44th Amendment allowed the President to send advice back once for reconsideration, but the reconsidered advice remains binding.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — the 44th Amendment did NOT remove the binding requirement; it merely ADDED a limited one-time reconsideration option, while keeping the RECONSIDERED advice fully binding on the President. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the 1997-99 President K.R. Narayanan episodes involving Article 356:
1. In October 1997, Narayanan returned a cabinet recommendation to impose President's Rule in Uttar Pradesh, and the cabinet subsequently decided not to proceed.
2. In September 1998, Narayanan similarly returned a recommendation regarding Bihar, and President's Rule was never imposed there.
3. Both episodes illustrate the President's power to send ministerial advice back once for reconsideration under the 44th Amendment framework.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — after Narayanan returned the Bihar recommendation, the cabinet RE-ADVISED the same course of action a few months later, and President's Rule WAS eventually imposed in Bihar in February 1999 (unlike the UP case, where the cabinet dropped the matter). Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's judicial and diplomatic powers:
1. The President appoints the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
2. Advice tendered by the Supreme Court when consulted by the President under Article 143 is binding on the President.
3. International treaties are negotiated and concluded on behalf of the President, subject to Parliament's approval.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — the Supreme Court's advice under Article 143 is explicitly NOT binding on the President; the President can seek it but remains free to act differently. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's military powers:
1. The President is the supreme commander of India's defence forces.
2. The President can declare war or conclude peace entirely at his/her own discretion, without needing Parliament's approval.
3. The President appoints the chiefs of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — declaring war or concluding peace is SUBJECT TO Parliament's approval, not a matter of the President's sole discretion. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the absolute veto's typical use cases:
1. It is usually exercised with respect to private members' bills.
2. It can be exercised for a government bill if the cabinet resigns after the bill's passage but before presidential assent, and the new cabinet advises withholding assent.
3. President Rajendra Prasad exercised absolute veto on the PEPSU Appropriation Bill after President's Rule in that state had been revoked before assent was given.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All three statements are correct — these are the book's own illustrative examples of when an absolute veto is typically exercised, showing it isn't limited to purely political private-member bills but can also arise from a genuine change in the government's own position on its own legislation.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why the Constitution designed a broad electoral college (Parliament plus state assemblies) for presidential elections rather than direct popular vote or Parliament-only election?
o: The design balances two competing goals — avoiding the anomaly of a directly-elected but merely ceremonial President (which direct popular election would create) while also ensuring the President represents the states as well as the Union (which Parliament-only election, dominated by one party, would fail to achieve)
The broad electoral college was chosen purely to reduce the cost of holding elections
Direct popular election was constitutionally prohibited by an earlier colonial-era law
The electoral college design was borrowed directly from the American presidential system
advanced.e: This dual rejection reveals the framers' careful balancing act: direct popular election was rejected because it would be inconsistent with the President's merely ceremonial, nominal-executive role (why give direct democratic legitimacy to an office with no real power?), while Parliament-only election was rejected because a single dominant party could then simply select 'its' candidate, undermining the President's role as a representative of BOTH the Union and the states equally — the broader electoral college threads this needle.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains the practical significance of the 44th Amendment Act, 1978's 'reconsideration' provision, as illustrated by the 1997 Uttar Pradesh and 1998-99 Bihar episodes?
o: It gives the President a genuine (though limited and non-final) check on ministerial advice — the President cannot permanently block advice, but can force the cabinet to pause, reflect, and potentially reverse course, as happened in the UP case, even though in the Bihar case the cabinet ultimately reasserted its original position and the President was bound to comply
It gives the President complete and final veto power over all cabinet decisions with no exceptions
It applies only to money bills and has no relevance to Article 356 proclamations
It was struck down by the Supreme Court shortly after being enacted and has no continuing legal effect
advanced.e: These two episodes perfectly illustrate the provision's REAL but LIMITED power: in the UP case, sending the recommendation back for reconsideration led the cabinet to change its mind (a genuine check in action), while in the Bihar case, the cabinet's re-advice after reconsideration was constitutionally BINDING on the President, who had no further recourse — showing the mechanism functions as a 'pause and reflect' check rather than an absolute veto.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why the D.C. Wadhwa case's ruling against repeated ordinance re-promulgation is significant beyond its specific facts about the Bihar Governor?
o: It establishes a broader constitutional principle that the ordinance power — designed for genuinely urgent, unforeseen situations — cannot be turned into a permanent substitute for regular legislative process through indefinite repetition, safeguarding the legislature's primary law-making role against executive overreach
It means ordinances can never be issued more than once on the same subject under any circumstances
It applies only to state Governors and has no bearing on the President's ordinance power under Article 123
It permanently abolished the ordinance-making power in India
advanced.e: The case's broader significance lies in preventing a structural workaround: since Article 123's ordinance power exists specifically for urgent, temporary situations pending Parliament's return, allowing INDEFINITE re-promulgation (as Bihar did for up to 14 years) would let the executive permanently bypass the legislature's law-making role entirely — the Court's ruling reinforces that ordinances remain a genuinely exceptional, temporary tool, not a parallel and permanent legislative track.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why the President's pardoning power under Article 72 is described as 'independent of the judiciary' even though it involves reviewing convictions and sentences?
o: Because the President does not sit as a court of appeal re-examining legal correctness, but instead exercises an executive check rooted in different considerations — correcting possible judicial errors and providing relief from unduly harsh sentences — operating on a fundamentally different basis than appellate judicial review
Because the President's decisions in pardon cases are always subject to full appellate review by the Supreme Court
Because the pardoning power was transferred entirely to the judiciary by a later constitutional amendment
Because Article 72 has never actually been used by any President
advanced.e: This 'independence' reflects a distinction in FUNCTION, not total insulation — the President's pardoning power serves purposes (correcting possible errors in the OPERATION of law, and affording relief from harshness) that are conceptually different from a court's role in determining legal guilt or innocence, which is why the Kehar Singh case held the President can adopt a different VIEW than the courts, even while acknowledging some (very narrow) judicial review remains possible for malafide, irrational, or discriminatory exercises of the power.

advanced.q: Which of the following best captures Dr. Ambedkar's core distinction between the American presidential system and India's parliamentary system, in describing the President's constitutional position?
o: In America, the President IS the chief executive with administration vested directly in him; in India, the President merely occupies a position like the English King — head of State but not of the Executive, bound by ministerial advice, functioning as a ceremonial 'seal' through which the nation's decisions are made known
Both systems are functionally identical, differing only in the title used for the head of state
In India, the President has MORE executive power than the American President
The American President is also bound by the advice of a council of ministers, just like India's President
advanced.e: Ambedkar's comparison is precise and deliberate: he explicitly notes that beyond the shared TITLE ('President'), there is 'nothing in common' between the two systems — America's President actually RULES as chief executive (and can dismiss any secretary at will), while India's President merely REPRESENTS the nation ceremonially, bound entirely by ministerial advice, unable to act contrary to or without it, so long as ministers command a parliamentary majority.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why the President's ordinance-making power is described as 'coextensive with Parliament's law-making power except as to duration'?
o: An ordinance can be issued only on subjects Parliament could legislate on, is subject to the same constitutional limits (including inability to abridge Fundamental Rights), and can do everything an Act can do substantively — but unlike an Act, it is inherently temporary, lapsing automatically unless converted into an Act by Parliament within the prescribed period
It means ordinances last exactly as long as Acts of Parliament with no time limit
It means the President can use ordinances to legislate on subjects even Parliament itself cannot address
It means ordinances are permanently exempt from any constitutional limitations, unlike parliamentary Acts
advanced.e: This phrase captures a precise substantive-versus-temporal distinction: in terms of WHAT can be legislated (subject matter, constitutional constraints like Fundamental Rights protection), an ordinance mirrors Parliament's own powers exactly — but in terms of HOW LONG it lasts, an ordinance is inherently provisional, automatically expiring within six weeks of Parliament's reassembly unless Parliament itself converts it into permanent legislation.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's election and electoral college:
1. Nominated members of state Legislative Councils participate in the President's election.
2. The Supreme Court has final authority to decide all doubts and disputes connected with the President's election.
3. An election cannot be challenged merely on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete due to vacancies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 1 is incorrect — nominated members of state Legislative Councils (and of Parliament) do NOT participate in the President's election; only elected members of Parliament and state/UT assemblies do. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

upsc.q:
Assertion (A): The President of India possesses a pocket veto that is, in practice, more powerful than that of the American President.
Reason (R): The Indian Constitution prescribes no time limit within which the President must act on a bill, whereas the American President must return a bill for reconsideration within 10 days.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above Assertion (A) and Reason (R)?
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
upsc.e: Both are true and R explains A — this exact comparison is captured in the book's remark that 'the pocket of the Indian President is bigger than that of the American President', precisely because of this absence of any prescribed deadline, illustrated concretely by Zail Singh's multi-year pocket veto of the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.

upsc.q:
With reference to the President's emergency powers, consider the following statements:
1. During a National Emergency, the President can suspend all Fundamental Rights without exception.
2. During President's Rule, the President can declare that state legislative powers shall be exercised by or under Parliament's authority.
3. During a Financial Emergency, the President can direct reduction of salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 1 is incorrect — the President CANNOT suspend the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) and the right to protection in respect of conviction for offences (Article 20), even during a National Emergency; these two rights remain protected. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the categories of bills requiring the President's prior recommendation or permission for introduction in Parliament:
1. A bill for the alteration of boundaries of states requires the President's recommendation.
2. A money bill requires the President's recommendation.
3. Every ordinary bill involving any government expenditure whatsoever, however minor, requires the President's prior recommendation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 overstates the rule — the specific category requiring recommendation is a bill involving expenditure specifically from the CONSOLIDATED FUND OF INDIA, not literally every bill with any expenditure implication whatsoever; the book lists this as one of seven specific categories, not a blanket rule for all spending-related bills. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Match List-I (Type of Veto) with List-II (Description) and select the correct answer using the code below.
List-I:
A. Absolute veto
B. Suspensive veto
C. Pocket veto
D. Qualified veto
List-II:
1. Overridable by legislature with a higher majority (not possessed by Indian President)
2. Withholding assent entirely, ending the bill
3. Taking no action on the bill for an indefinite period
4. Returning the bill, overridable by an ordinary majority on re-passage
upsc.e: Absolute veto = withholding assent entirely (2); suspensive veto = returning for reconsideration, overridable by ordinary majority (4); pocket veto = indefinite inaction (3); qualified veto = overridable only by higher majority, not possessed by the Indian President (1). Correct code: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the differences between the President's and Governor's pardoning powers:
1. The President can pardon sentences by court martial; the Governor cannot.
2. The President can pardon a death sentence; the Governor cannot pardon it but CAN suspend, remit, or commute it.
3. This means the President and Governor have no overlapping powers whatsoever regarding death sentences.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — the President and Governor actually DO have CONCURRENT (overlapping) power specifically regarding suspension, remission, and commutation of a death sentence; it is only the full PARDON of a death sentence that remains exclusively with the President. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's situational discretion:
1. The President can exercise discretion in appointing a Prime Minister when no party has a clear Lok Sabha majority.
2. The President can dismiss a council of ministers on his/her own personal assessment, without requiring it to first prove confidence on the floor of the House.
3. The President can exercise discretion in dissolving the Lok Sabha if the council of ministers has lost its majority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 2 overstates the President's discretion — dismissal of the council of ministers arises specifically when it CANNOT PROVE confidence on the floor of the Lok Sabha (i.e., after a floor test or failure to face one), not based merely on the President's own subjective assessment. Statements 1 and 3 correctly describe genuine situational-discretion scenarios.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's five forms of pardoning power:
1. Commutation substitutes a lighter form of punishment for a harsher one.
2. Respite awards a lesser sentence due to special facts such as physical disability or pregnancy.
3. Reprieve permanently cancels a death sentence rather than merely staying its execution temporarily.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — reprieve is only a TEMPORARY stay of execution (to allow time to seek pardon or commutation), not a permanent cancellation of the sentence; permanent cancellation is what 'pardon' itself achieves. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
With reference to the President's veto power over Central legislation (Table 18.2), consider the following statements:
1. For ordinary bills, the President can ratify, reject, or return the bill.
2. For money bills, the President can ratify or reject the bill, but cannot return it.
3. For constitutional amendment bills, the President can ratify, reject, or return the bill, exactly as with ordinary bills.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — for constitutional amendment bills, the President can ONLY ratify (give assent); rejection and return are not available options, unlike with ordinary bills. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the formula for calculating the value of votes in the presidential electoral college:
1. Every elected MLA's vote value depends on dividing the state's population by the total elected assembly seats, then dividing by 1,000.
2. Every elected MP's vote value is calculated by dividing the aggregate value of all state MLA votes by the total number of elected MPs.
3. This system is designed to ensure uniformity in representation across states and parity between the states as a whole and the Union.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — the book explicitly states the Constitution provides for 'uniformity in the scale of representation of different states as well as parity between the states as a whole and the Union', which this vote-value formula is specifically designed to achieve.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the security deposit and forfeiture rules for presidential candidates:
1. Every candidate must deposit ₹15,000 with the Reserve Bank of India.
2. This deposit is forfeited if the candidate fails to secure one-sixth of the votes polled.
3. Before 1997, the security deposit was ₹2,500, and it was increased specifically to discourage non-serious candidates.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — alongside raising the number of required proposers/seconders from 10 to 50 each, the 1997 amendment to the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 raised both the deposit amount and this one-sixth forfeiture threshold specifically to deter frivolous candidacies.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's salary and pension provisions:
1. In 2018, Parliament increased the President's salary from ₹1.50 lakh to ₹5 lakh per month.
2. In 2008, the pension of a retired President was increased to 50% of his/her salary per month.
3. The spouse of a deceased President is entitled to a family pension at the rate of 50% of the pension of a retired President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — these figures trace the escalating financial provisions made for the President and their family, reflecting periodic parliamentary revisions to compensation and post-retirement benefits for this office.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's personal immunity from legal proceedings:
1. The President is immune from any criminal proceedings during the term of office, even in respect of personal acts.
2. The President cannot be arrested or imprisoned during the term of office.
3. Civil proceedings can never be instituted against the President in respect of personal acts, even after giving notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — civil proceedings CAN be instituted against the President during the term of office in respect of personal acts, but only AFTER giving two months' advance notice; it is not an absolute, permanent immunity from civil suits. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about vacancy scenarios and the mechanism to prevent an 'interregnum' in the presidency:
1. If a delay occurs in conducting a new presidential election due to any reason, the outgoing President continues in office beyond the five-year term until a successor assumes charge.
2. In this specific interregnum-prevention scenario, the Vice-President gets the opportunity to act as President instead of the outgoing President continuing.
3. If the vacancy instead arises from resignation, removal, or death, the Vice-President does act as President until a new President is elected.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — in this SPECIFIC scenario (delay in conducting an election to replace a President whose TERM is expiring), the OUTGOING PRESIDENT continues, and the Vice-President does NOT get the opportunity to act as President; the Vice-President's acting role is reserved for the DIFFERENT scenario of resignation/removal/death. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the D.C. Wadhwa case (1986) concerning the Bihar Governor's ordinance-making practice:
1. Between 1967 and 1981, the Bihar Governor promulgated 256 ordinances.
2. These ordinances were kept in force for periods ranging from one to fourteen years through repeated re-promulgation.
3. The Supreme Court held that this practice amounted to violation of the Constitution and that such repromulgated ordinances are liable to be struck down.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — the sheer scale (256 ordinances) and duration (up to fourteen years without ever being converted into proper legislation) of this practice is precisely what led the Supreme Court to intervene and establish that ordinance power cannot substitute for genuine legislative action.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's power to seek advice from the Supreme Court under Article 143:
1. The President can seek the Supreme Court's advice on any question of law or fact.
2. The advice tendered by the Supreme Court under this provision is binding on the President.
3. This is classified as one of the President's judicial powers and functions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — the Supreme Court's advice under Article 143 is explicitly NOT binding on the President, who remains free to act differently after receiving it. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's executive powers relating to appointments:
1. The President appoints the Attorney General of India and determines his/her remuneration.
2. The President appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General, the Chief Election Commissioner, and the Chairman and members of the UPSC.
3. The Attorney General holds office for a fixed five-year term, unlike other presidential appointees who serve at pleasure.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — the Attorney General holds office DURING THE PLEASURE OF THE PRESIDENT, with no fixed five-year term specified; this differs from claiming a fixed term distinct from other appointees. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's power to seek information from the Prime Minister:
1. The President can seek any information relating to the administration of Union affairs and proposals for legislation from the Prime Minister.
2. The President can require the Prime Minister to submit for the council of ministers' consideration any matter decided by a single minister but not yet considered by the full council.
3. These powers are entirely discretionary and require no cooperation from the Prime Minister to be exercised effectively.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 overstates presidential autonomy here — while the President CAN make these requests, the underlying constitutional design (Article 78, mirrored in these executive powers) presumes cooperative compliance from the Prime Minister as part of the ordinary functioning of aid-and-advice, not a purely unilateral presidential capability. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's diplomatic and military powers:
1. International treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded on behalf of the President, subject to Parliament's approval.
2. The President, as supreme commander of the defence forces, personally leads military operations during wartime.
3. The President can declare war or conclude peace, subject to the approval of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — while the President holds the ceremonial title of supreme commander and appoints the service chiefs, the book does not describe the President as personally leading military operations; actual command and operational leadership rests with the armed forces' own chain of command. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the President's power to appoint a commission for backward classes and an inter-state council:
1. The President can appoint a commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes.
2. The President can appoint an inter-state council to promote Centre-state and inter-state cooperation.
3. Both of these powers are classified under the President's judicial powers rather than executive powers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — both the backward classes commission and the inter-state council appointment powers are classified under the President's EXECUTIVE powers and functions, not judicial powers. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

title: Vice-President of India
desc: Election, qualifications, term, removal and vacancy of the Vice-President, dual role as ex-officio Rajya Sabha Chairman and acting President, and a comparison with the American Vice-President

basic.q: On whose office is the Indian Vice-President's office modelled?
basic.e: The Vice-President's office is modelled on the American Vice-President. Both hold the second-highest office in their respective countries and both chair the upper house of their legislature (Rajya Sabha in India, Senate in the USA) — though, as the chapter later explains, there is a crucial difference in what happens when the presidency itself falls vacant.

basic.q: Which body constitutes the electoral college for the Vice-President's election?
o: Members of both Houses of Parliament (elected and nominated)
Only elected members of the Lok Sabha
Members of Parliament and all state legislative assemblies
Only elected members of both Houses of Parliament
basic.e: The Vice-President's electoral college consists of all members of both Houses of Parliament, both elected and nominated — unlike the President's electoral college, which includes only ELECTED members of Parliament plus elected state/UT assembly members, and excludes nominated members entirely.

basic.q: Which constitutional amendment did away with the original, cumbersome procedure of electing the Vice-President via a joint meeting of both Houses of Parliament?
basic.e: The 11th Amendment Act, 1961 simplified the process, moving away from requiring a joint sitting of both Houses assembled together for the Vice-President's election.

basic.q: According to Dr. Ambedkar, why does the Vice-President's electoral college NOT include state legislative assembly members, unlike the President's?
o: Because the Vice-President's normal function is only to preside over the Rajya Sabha, and only rarely and temporarily assumes presidential duties, so state legislatures need not have a voice
Because state legislatures were constitutionally barred from participating in any Union-level elections
Because the Vice-President represents only the Union government, not the states, in a permanent capacity
Because the Constituent Assembly ran out of time to include this provision
basic.e: Ambedkar explained that since the Vice-President's NORMAL role is merely presiding over the Rajya Sabha (not administering the Centre and states like the President does), and assuming presidential duties happens only rarely and temporarily, it was not considered necessary to give state legislatures a voice in this particular election — unlike the President's election, where the President's authority genuinely extends over both Centre and states.

basic.q: What voting system is used for the Vice-President's election, matching the President's election method?
o: Proportional representation by single transferable vote, via secret ballot
Electoral college weighted voting without transferable preferences
basic.e: Like the President's election, the Vice-President is elected via proportional representation by single transferable vote, using secret ballot — even though only Parliament members (not state legislators) form the electoral college.

basic.q: Which authority has final jurisdiction to decide all doubts and disputes connected with the Vice-President's election?
basic.e: The Supreme Court has final authority over such disputes — mirroring the exact same rule that applies to presidential election disputes. As with the President, a Vice-President's election cannot be challenged merely because the electoral college had vacancies at the time.

basic.q: What is the minimum age required to be eligible for election as Vice-President?
basic.e: A candidate must have completed 35 years of age — identical to the minimum age for the President, and higher than the 25-year minimum for Lok Sabha membership.

basic.q: For which House must a Vice-President candidate be qualified for election as a member?
o: Either House, at the candidate's choice
No specific House qualification is required
basic.e: A candidate must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha — fittingly, since the Vice-President's primary constitutional function is to serve as the Rajya Sabha's ex-officio Chairman.

basic.q: How many electors must subscribe as proposers and seconders for a valid Vice-Presidential nomination?
basic.e: A Vice-Presidential nomination requires 20 proposers and 20 seconders — notably fewer than the 50 each required for a presidential nomination, reflecting the smaller, Parliament-only electoral college for this office.

basic.q: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice-President?
o: The President, or a person appointed by the President for this purpose
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
basic.e: The President (or someone appointed by the President for this purpose) administers the Vice-President's oath — a notable contrast to the President's OWN oath, which is instead administered by the Chief Justice of India.

basic.q: What is the term of office of the Vice-President?
o: Term coincides with the President's term
basic.e: The Vice-President holds office for five years from entering office — the same duration as the President's term, though the two terms need not run concurrently or be synchronised with each other.

basic.q: By what process is the Vice-President removed from office, and does it require formal impeachment like the President?
o: By a Rajya Sabha resolution (effective majority) agreed to by the Lok Sabha (simple majority); no formal impeachment is required
By formal impeachment requiring two-thirds majority in both Houses, identical to the President's removal process
By a simple majority resolution passed by the Lok Sabha alone
By direct dismissal by the President without any parliamentary involvement
basic.e: Unlike the President, the Vice-President's removal does NOT require formal impeachment — it needs only a resolution passed by a majority of ALL THEN MEMBERS of the Rajya Sabha (an 'effective majority') and AGREED TO by the Lok Sabha via simple majority. Notably, this resolution can be introduced ONLY in the Rajya Sabha.

basic.q: How many days' advance notice must be given before a resolution for the Vice-President's removal can be moved in the Rajya Sabha?
basic.e: At least 14 days' advance notice must be given before such a resolution can be moved — the same 14-day notice period the book also cites for a special Lok Sabha sitting to disapprove continuation of a National Emergency.

basic.q: Does the Constitution specify any grounds for the Vice-President's removal from office?
o: No, the Constitution does not mention any ground for removal
Yes, only 'violation of the Constitution' as with the President
Yes, only proven misbehaviour or incapacity
Yes, only conviction for a criminal offence
basic.e: Notably, no ground is mentioned in the Constitution for the Vice-President's removal — unlike the President, whose removal is tied specifically to 'violation of the Constitution'. This gives Parliament considerable latitude in deciding when removal is warranted.

basic.q: Is the Vice-President eligible for re-election, and if so, for how many terms?
o: Yes, for any number of terms
Yes, but only for a maximum of two terms
Yes, but only once, for a total of two terms
basic.e: The Vice-President is eligible for re-election for any number of terms, just like the President. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan is cited as an example of someone actually elected to a second term as Vice-President.

basic.q: What are the Vice-President's two main constitutional functions?
o: Acting as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and acting as President during a presidential vacancy
Leading the ruling party in Parliament, and chairing the Union Cabinet
Acting as Deputy Prime Minister, and heading the Planning Commission
Presiding over the Lok Sabha, and heading the Election Commission
basic.e: The Vice-President's two functions are: acting as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (with powers similar to the Lok Sabha Speaker), and acting as President when a vacancy arises in that office due to resignation, impeachment, death, or otherwise.

basic.q: For a maximum of how long can the Vice-President act as President following a vacancy in the President's office?
basic.e: The Vice-President can act as President for a maximum of six months, within which a new President must be elected — aligning with the broader constitutional rule that a presidential vacancy (from resignation, removal, or death) must be filled within six months.

basic.q: While the Vice-President is acting as President, who performs the duties of the Rajya Sabha Chairman in their place?
o: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
No one; the Rajya Sabha is left leaderless during this period
basic.e: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha takes over these duties, since the Vice-President cannot simultaneously act as President and perform the Chairman's role — the two positions are mutually exclusive during this period.

basic.q: What salary/allowance does the Vice-President draw while acting as President, as opposed to while serving as Rajya Sabha Chairman?
o: The salary and allowance of the President, not of the Rajya Sabha Chairman
No salary at all during this period, as a mark of the office's transitional status
Double salary, combining both offices' emoluments
The same Rajya Sabha Chairman's salary, unchanged
basic.e: While acting as President, the Vice-President receives the President's salary and allowances, NOT the Rajya Sabha Chairman's — reflecting that during this period, they are functionally performing the President's role and are compensated accordingly.

basic.q: Who was the first Vice-President of India to die in office?
basic.e: Krishna Kant was the first Vice-President to die while in office. Separately, when Presidents Dr. Zakir Husain and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office, their respective sitting Vice-Presidents (V.V. Giri and B.D. Jatti) stepped in to act as President.

basic.q: Why do some scholars refer to the Vice-President as 'His Superfluous Highness'?
o: Because the Constitution has not assigned the office any truly significant, independent function beyond the two limited roles described
Because the office was abolished shortly after independence and later restored
Because the Vice-President has no salary or official residence
Because the Vice-President is not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution's text
basic.e: This somewhat dismissive label reflects the office's genuinely LIMITED constitutional role — beyond presiding over the Rajya Sabha and occasionally, temporarily, acting as President, the Vice-President has no significant independent function, unlike say the American Vice-President who actually SUCCEEDS to the presidency for the remainder of the term when it falls vacant.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements comparing the electoral colleges of the President and Vice-President:
1. The Vice-President's electoral college includes nominated members of Parliament, while the President's does not.
2. The Vice-President's electoral college includes elected members of state legislative assemblies, while the President's does not.
3. Both electoral colleges use the same voting system: proportional representation by single transferable vote.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect and reverses the actual rule — it is the PRESIDENT's electoral college that includes elected state assembly members, while the VICE-PRESIDENT's electoral college does NOT include any state legislators at all, being confined to Parliament. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's removal process:
1. The removal resolution can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
2. The resolution requires a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha, and simple majority agreement from the Lok Sabha.
3. At least 14 days' advance notice must be given before such a resolution can be moved.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is incorrect — the removal resolution can be introduced ONLY in the Rajya Sabha, not in either House at the mover's choice. Statements 2 and 3 correctly describe the majority requirements and notice period.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about vacancy-filling timelines for the Vice-President's office:
1. If the vacancy arises from the expiry of the sitting Vice-President's term, the election must be held before the term expires.
2. If the vacancy arises from resignation, removal, or death, the Constitution specifies the election must be held within six months, exactly like the President's vacancy rule.
3. A newly elected Vice-President, in either scenario, serves a full five-year term from the date of assuming office.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — for the Vice-President, the Constitution simply requires the election be held 'as soon as possible', without specifying a fixed six-month deadline as it does for the President's vacancy. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's dual roles and compensation:
1. The Constitution has fixed specific emoluments for the Vice-President in his/her capacity as Vice-President.
2. The Vice-President draws a regular salary specifically in the capacity of ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
3. While acting as President, the Vice-President receives the President's salary rather than the Chairman's salary.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is incorrect — the Constitution has NOT fixed any separate emoluments for the Vice-President qua Vice-President; salary is drawn only through the Rajya Sabha Chairmanship role (or the President's salary when acting as President). Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements comparing the Indian and American Vice-Presidents:
1. The American Vice-President succeeds to the presidency and completes the unexpired term when it falls vacant.
2. The Indian Vice-President similarly succeeds to and completes the unexpired presidential term when it falls vacant.
3. Both offices were created partly to maintain political continuity in their respective countries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — the Indian Vice-President does NOT succeed to the office; they merely ACT as President temporarily (maximum six months) until a fresh election is held, unlike the American system where the Vice-President actually becomes President for the remainder of the term. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about instances of the Vice-President discharging presidential functions:
1. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan discharged the functions of the President in 1960 when President Rajendra Prasad was on a tour to the USSR.
2. This particular instance involved a vacancy in the President's office due to resignation.
3. Dr. Radhakrishnan again discharged these functions in 1961 when the President was ill.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — this was not a VACANCY at all; it was a case of the sitting President being temporarily UNABLE to discharge functions (due to travel/illness), a distinct scenario from an actual vacancy caused by resignation, death, or removal. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's oath of office:
1. In the oath, the Vice-President swears to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India.
2. The Vice-President's oath also includes a promise to devote himself/herself to the service and well-being of the people of India, identical to the President's oath.
3. The oath is administered by the President or a person appointed by the President for this purpose.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — the Vice-President's oath is narrower, covering only allegiance to the Constitution and faithful discharge of office duties; it does NOT include the specific 'service and well-being of the people' clause that appears in the PRESIDENT's oath. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's conditions of office:
1. The Vice-President should not be a member of either House of Parliament or a state legislature.
2. If a sitting MP is elected Vice-President, they are deemed to have vacated their parliamentary seat automatically upon entering office.
3. The Vice-President is permitted to simultaneously hold one other office of profit, unlike the President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — like the President, the Vice-President is also prohibited from holding ANY other office of profit; there is no special permission for one additional office. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why the Vice-President's removal process, unlike the President's impeachment, does not require a formal 'impeachment' procedure?
o: The Vice-President's constitutional role is comparatively limited (chairing the Rajya Sabha, occasionally acting as President) rather than being the nation's head of state, so the framers designed a comparatively lighter, faster removal mechanism (Rajya Sabha resolution plus Lok Sabha agreement) proportionate to the office's lesser constitutional weight, without needing a quasi-judicial charge-and-investigation process
The Vice-President has no real constitutional protections at all and can be dismissed by the Prime Minister alone
Impeachment was considered unconstitutional by the Supreme Court and removed from all removal procedures
The Vice-President's removal process is actually more stringent than the President's impeachment process
advanced.e: This lighter-touch removal design reflects the office's comparatively lesser constitutional significance — since the Vice-President is not the head of state exercising ongoing executive authority (merely presiding over the Rajya Sabha and rarely, temporarily acting as President), a full quasi-judicial impeachment process (with formal charges, 14-day notice, investigation by the other House, and two-thirds majorities in BOTH Houses) was not considered necessary; instead, a more straightforward resolution process suffices.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why Dr. Ambedkar considered it unnecessary to give state legislatures a voice in electing the Vice-President, despite giving them a voice in electing the President?
o: The Vice-President's authority does not ordinarily extend over Centre-state administration the way the President's does; the Vice-President's role is confined mainly to presiding over the Rajya Sabha, with presidential functions assumed only rarely and temporarily, making the broader Centre-state representative logic used for the President's election inapplicable
State legislatures were considered too politically unstable to be trusted with electing the Vice-President
The Vice-President was originally intended to be appointed rather than elected at all
Ambedkar believed the Vice-President's office would eventually be abolished, making the electoral college design irrelevant
advanced.e: Ambedkar's reasoning directly ties electoral college composition to the SCOPE of the office's authority — since the President's power genuinely extends over both Union and state administration (justifying state legislature participation for balanced representation), while the Vice-President's NORMAL function is narrowly confined to the Rajya Sabha (a purely Union-level body), and presidential functions are assumed only exceptionally and temporarily, there was no equivalent need to involve the states in this particular election.

advanced.q: Which of the following best captures the functional difference underlying the label 'His Superfluous Highness' as applied to the Vice-President, compared to the American Vice-President?
o: The American Vice-President has a genuine constitutional destiny — automatic succession to a vacant presidency for the remainder of the term — giving the office real, guaranteed future significance, while the Indian Vice-President's role is limited to routine legislative presiding functions and only a brief, temporary caretaker role during a vacancy, with no guarantee of ever becoming President in their own right
Both offices are functionally identical, and the label is purely a matter of translation from English
The American Vice-President has no legislative role at all, unlike the Indian Vice-President
The label refers to the fact that India has never actually filled the office of Vice-President since independence
advanced.e: The 'superfluous' characterisation stems specifically from the CONTRAST in ultimate constitutional destiny: the American Vice-President's role includes a genuine guarantee of stepping into the full presidency (for the remainder of the term) should it fall vacant, while the Indian Vice-President's role during a vacancy is explicitly temporary and caretaker-only (max six months, with no automatic succession) — leaving the office's day-to-day significance limited mainly to a legislative presiding function that, while useful, lacks the weight of guaranteed executive succession.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's qualifications and disqualifications:
1. A person must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha.
2. A sitting Governor of a state is disqualified from being a Vice-Presidential candidate for holding an office of profit.
3. A sitting Vice-President seeking re-election is not deemed to hold an office of profit for this purpose.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 2 is incorrect — a sitting Governor, like a sitting President/Vice-President or a Union/state minister, is specifically NOT deemed to hold an office of profit, and remains eligible as a candidate. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

upsc.q:
Assertion (A): The Vice-President's electoral college is smaller and narrower in composition than the President's electoral college.
Reason (R): The Vice-President's normal constitutional function (presiding over the Rajya Sabha) does not extend to Centre-state administration the way the President's functions do, so state legislature participation was not considered necessary for this election.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above Assertion (A) and Reason (R)?
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
upsc.e: Both are true and R explains A — Ambedkar's own stated reasoning in the Constituent Assembly directly supports this causal link between the scope of an office's functions and the design of its electoral college.

upsc.q:
With reference to the differences between the Indian and American Vice-Presidents, consider the following statements:
1. The American Vice-President completes the unexpired presidential term upon a vacancy, while the Indian Vice-President only acts as President temporarily.
2. Both Vice-Presidents share the common function of chairing the upper house of their respective legislatures.
3. The Indian Vice-President's office was created for reasons entirely unrelated to political continuity.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — the book explicitly states the office was created 'with a view to maintain the political continuity of the Indian State', directly contradicting the claim that continuity was unrelated to its creation. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President acting as President versus discharging the President's functions:
1. The Vice-President 'acts as President' specifically when a vacancy occurs due to resignation, removal, death, or otherwise.
2. The Vice-President 'discharges the functions' of the President when the sitting President is temporarily unable to act due to absence or illness, without any vacancy occurring.
3. In both scenarios, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha takes over the Vice-President's chairmanship duties.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — this distinguishes two related but conceptually different scenarios (an actual VACANCY versus a temporary INABILITY without vacancy), while the practical consequence for Rajya Sabha leadership (Deputy Chairman stepping in) is the same in both cases.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about notable facts in the history of the Vice-Presidential office:
1. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was elected unopposed on more than one occasion.
2. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was also elected for a second term as Vice-President.
3. M. Hidayatullah is recorded as having been elected unopposed as Vice-President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct, drawing directly from the book's election table — Dr. Radhakrishnan was elected unopposed twice (elections 1 and 2) and also served a second term; M. Hidayatullah was also elected unopposed (election 7), showing unopposed elections have occurred more than once in Vice-Presidential history.

upsc.q:
Match List-I (Article) with List-II (Subject Matter) and select the correct answer using the code below.
List-I:
A. Article 63
B. Article 64
C. Article 66
D. Article 69
List-II:
1. Election of Vice-President
2. The Vice-President of India
3. Oath or affirmation by the Vice-President
4. The Vice-President to be ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States
upsc.e: Article 63 establishes the office of Vice-President; Article 64 makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha); Article 66 deals with election of the Vice-President; Article 69 deals with the oath or affirmation. Correct code: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about unopposed elections to the office of Vice-President:
1. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was elected unopposed on two separate occasions.
2. M. Hidayatullah was also elected unopposed.
3. Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma was elected unopposed as Vice-President as well.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct, based on the book's election table — Dr. Radhakrishnan (twice), M. Hidayatullah, and Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma were all elected unopposed as Vice-President at different points in India's history, showing unopposed elections have occurred multiple times for this office.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about Mohammad Hamid Ansari's tenure as Vice-President:
1. He served two consecutive terms as Vice-President.
2. His two main rival candidates across these two elections were Najma Heptullah and Jaswant Singh respectively.
3. He is the only Vice-President in India's history to have served more than one term.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was ALSO elected for a second term as Vice-President (as explicitly noted in the book's footnotes), meaning Hamid Ansari is not the only one to have served more than one term. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about salary revisions for the Vice-President (in the capacity of Rajya Sabha Chairman):
1. In 2018, Parliament increased the Chairman's salary from ₹1.25 lakh to ₹4 lakh per month.
2. This revision was made through the Finance Act, 2018, with effect from 1st January 2016.
3. This revision amended the Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament Act, 1953.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — this mirrors the same 2018 Finance Act mechanism (with retrospective effect from 2016) used to revise the President's salary, applied here specifically to the Rajya Sabha Chairman's compensation, which is how the Vice-President is actually paid.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's Pension (Amendment) Act, 2008:
1. It increased the pension of a retired Vice-President from ₹20,000 per month to 50% of his/her salary per month.
2. This amendment updated the Vice-President's Pension Act, 1997.
3. It also introduced, for the first time, any pension entitlement whatsoever for a retired Vice-President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — the 2008 Act INCREASED an already-existing pension (from ₹20,000/month to 50% of salary), it did not introduce pension entitlement for the first time, since the underlying Vice-President's Pension Act already existed from 1997. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Assertion (A): Dr. S. Radhakrishnan discharged the functions of the President on two separate occasions in 1960 and 1961.
Reason (R): Both occasions arose because the sitting President, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, was temporarily unable to discharge his functions — once due to a foreign tour and once due to illness — rather than because of any vacancy in the presidential office.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above Assertion (A) and Reason (R)?
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
upsc.e: Both are true and R explains A — Radhakrishnan's 1960 (15-day USSR tour) and 1961 (illness) instances were both cases of TEMPORARY presidential inability without any actual vacancy, distinguishing them from the 'acting as President' scenario that applies during genuine vacancies.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the historical timeline of Vice-Presidents who later became President:
1. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan served as Vice-President before becoming President.
2. V.V. Giri and B.D. Jatti both acted as President following the deaths of sitting Presidents while they were Vice-President.
3. R. Venkataraman also transitioned from Vice-President to President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — this reflects a historically common career pathway in Indian politics, where several individuals (Radhakrishnan, Venkataraman, and others across subsequent decades) served as Vice-President before later being elected President in their own right.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the removal procedure for the Vice-President compared to ordinary legislative resolutions:
1. The removal resolution requires a majority of ALL THEN MEMBERS of the Rajya Sabha, which is a stricter threshold than a simple majority of members present and voting.
2. The Lok Sabha's agreement to such a resolution requires only a simple majority of members present and voting.
3. This asymmetry means the Rajya Sabha's threshold for removal is actually higher than the Lok Sabha's.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — an 'effective majority' (majority of ALL members, not just those present and voting) is indeed a stricter threshold than an ordinary simple majority, meaning the Rajya Sabha's bar for initiating removal is set deliberately higher than the Lok Sabha's bar for concurring with it.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the timing flexibility in filling Vice-Presidential vacancies:
1. When a vacancy arises from the expiry of the sitting Vice-President's term, the election must be completed before the term expires.
2. When a vacancy arises from resignation, removal, or death, the Constitution requires the election to be held 'as soon as possible', without a fixed numerical deadline.
3. This contrasts with the President's vacancy rules, which do specify a fixed six-month deadline for elections following resignation, removal, or death.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — this is a genuine textual difference between Articles 62 (President) and 68 (Vice-President): the President's vacancy-filling timeline is fixed at six months, while the Vice-President's is left to the more flexible 'as soon as possible' standard.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the Vice-President's role during the President's temporary inability to act:
1. This scenario is governed by a different constitutional mechanism than the 'acting as President' scenario triggered by an actual vacancy.
2. During this temporary-inability scenario, the Vice-President is also barred from performing the duties of the Rajya Sabha Chairman.
3. The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha steps in during both the vacancy-based 'acting as President' scenario and the temporary-inability scenario.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — regardless of WHICH scenario triggers the Vice-President's presidential duties (genuine vacancy or temporary inability), the practical consequence for the Rajya Sabha's leadership is identical: the Deputy Chairman takes over chairmanship duties in both cases.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements comparing the electoral college compositions for the President and Vice-President with respect to nominated members:
1. Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha DO participate in electing the Vice-President.
2. Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha do NOT participate in electing the President.
3. This asymmetry directly reflects the difference in scope between the two offices' normal constitutional functions, as explained by Dr. Ambedkar.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct and consolidate the chapter's central theme — nominated MPs vote for the Vice-President but not the President, an asymmetry Ambedkar explicitly tied to the narrower, Rajya-Sabha-focused scope of the Vice-President's ordinary functions versus the President's broader Centre-and-state authority.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the office of Vice-President and the historical precedent it maintains:
1. The office was created with a view to maintain the political continuity of the Indian State.
2. Despite this stated purpose, the Constitution assigns the Vice-President no truly significant independent function in that specific capacity.
3. This combination has led some scholars to use the somewhat dismissive label 'His Superfluous Highness' for the office.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct and directly connect the office's stated purpose (political continuity) with the critical assessment of its actual, limited constitutional weight — a tension the book explicitly draws out through this scholarly label.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the 11th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1961's effect on the Vice-Presidential election procedure:
1. Before this amendment, the Vice-President was elected by the two Houses of Parliament assembled at a joint meeting.
2. This joint-meeting procedure was described in the book as 'cumbersome'.
3. The amendment eliminated the joint-meeting requirement while retaining an electoral college confined to Parliament (both Houses, but not assembled jointly).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: All three statements are correct — the 11th Amendment simplified the PROCEDURE (removing the need for an actual joint sitting) while the electoral college's fundamental COMPOSITION (both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated members) remained essentially the same as before.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about Krishna Kant's significance in Vice-Presidential history:
1. He was the first Vice-President to die while in office.
2. His death necessitated the application of the Constitution's vacancy-filling provisions specific to the Vice-President's office.
3. Following his death, a Vice-President-elect automatically succeeded him without a fresh election, mirroring the American system.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — there is no such 'automatic succession' mechanism for the Vice-Presidency in India; a fresh election (to be held 'as soon as possible') is required to fill any Vice-Presidential vacancy, including one caused by death, with no equivalent to American-style automatic succession even for this office. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

upsc.q:
Consider the following statements about the overall structural relationship between the Vice-President's two constitutional roles:
1. The Rajya Sabha Chairmanship role is a permanent, ongoing function throughout the full five-year term.
2. The 'acting as President' role is an exceptional, temporary function that arises only under specific triggering conditions and is capped at six months.
3. Both roles can be exercised simultaneously by the Vice-President at the same time.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
upsc.e: Statement 3 is incorrect — the two roles are explicitly MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE; while acting as President, the Vice-President does NOT perform Rajya Sabha Chairman duties (which fall to the Deputy Chairman instead), meaning both roles cannot be exercised simultaneously. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

title: Prime Minister & Council of Ministers
desc: Appointment, oath, term and powers of the Prime Minister; role descriptions and relationship with the President; caretaker governments; the constitutional provisions, composition, responsibility (collective, individual, and the absence of legal responsibility) of the Council of Ministers; the Cabinet versus Council of Ministers distinction; and the Kitchen Cabinet

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution simply states that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President, without specifying a detailed procedure?
basic.e: Article 75 states only that the Prime Minister 'shall be appointed by the President' — the Constitution contains no detailed procedure. In practice, convention requires the President to appoint the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha, with genuine personal discretion arising only when no party has a clear majority.

basic.q: Who was the first Prime Minister appointed through the President's personal discretion, following the fall of the Morarji Desai government in 1979?
basic.e: President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy appointed Charan Singh (the coalition leader) as PM in 1979 after Morarji Desai's Janata Party government fell — the first time this presidential discretion was exercised, since no party had a clear Lok Sabha majority at that point.

basic.q: Which President appointed Rajiv Gandhi as Prime Minister in 1984, ignoring the earlier precedent of appointing a caretaker Prime Minister, following Indira Gandhi's assassination?
basic.e: President Zail Singh made this discretionary appointment immediately, departing from the earlier practice of appointing a caretaker PM (as had been done twice before, with Gulzari Lal Nanda, following the deaths of Nehru and Shastri) — the Congress parliamentary party later unanimously elected Rajiv Gandhi as its own leader.

basic.q: According to a 1980 Delhi High Court ruling, must a person prove majority support in the Lok Sabha BEFORE being appointed Prime Minister?
o: No, the President can appoint first and then ask for a confidence vote within a reasonable period
Yes, majority proof is mandatory before any appointment
Yes, but only if more than one candidate stakes a claim
No, majority proof is never required at any stage
basic.e: The 1980 Delhi High Court ruling held that the Constitution does NOT require proving majority BEFORE appointment — the President may appoint first and then require a confidence vote within a reasonable period, a practice followed for PMs like Charan Singh (1979), V.P. Singh (1989), and several others listed in the book.

basic.q: According to a 1996 Supreme Court ruling, for how long can a person who is not a member of either House of Parliament serve as Prime Minister?
o: Six months, within which they must become a member of either House
One year, with automatic disqualification thereafter
Indefinitely, as membership is not required for PM
Three months, with a possible one-time extension
basic.e: The 1996 Supreme Court ruling held such a person can serve for a maximum of six months, within which they must become a member of either House — otherwise they cease to be Prime Minister, mirroring the same six-month rule that applies to ordinary ministers.

basic.q: Which two oaths does the President administer to the Prime Minister before he/she enters office?
o: Oath of office and oath of secrecy
Oath of allegiance and oath of loyalty
Oath of office only, with no secrecy oath
Oath of secrecy and oath of impartiality
basic.e: The President administers the oath of office and oath of secrecy — the same combination administered to any Union minister. In the oath of secrecy, the PM specifically swears not to reveal matters brought under consideration except as required for official duties.

basic.q: On whose pleasure does the Prime Minister hold office, and can the President dismiss the PM at any time?
o: The President's pleasure, but the President cannot dismiss a PM who enjoys Lok Sabha majority support
The President's pleasure, and the President can dismiss the PM at any time for any reason
Parliament's pleasure exclusively, with no presidential role
The Prime Minister's own discretion, serving until voluntary resignation
basic.e: The PM holds office during the President's pleasure in name, but in substance this is constrained by convention — as long as the PM enjoys Lok Sabha majority support, the President CANNOT dismiss them; dismissal (or resignation) becomes appropriate only once that confidence is actually lost.

basic.q: Who recommends persons for appointment as ministers, whom the President can then appoint?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
basic.e: The Prime Minister recommends ministers, and the President can appoint ONLY those persons the PM recommends — this is one of the PM's core powers in relation to the council of ministers, alongside allocating/reshuffling portfolios and asking ministers to resign.

basic.q: What happens to the entire council of ministers when the Prime Minister resigns or dies?
o: The council of ministers is automatically dissolved
Only the Prime Minister's position becomes vacant; other ministers continue
The Deputy Prime Minister automatically becomes the new Prime Minister
The council continues functioning under the senior-most cabinet minister
basic.e: The entire council of ministers is automatically dissolved when the PM resigns or dies, generating a vacuum — this differs sharply from the resignation or death of any OTHER minister, which merely creates a vacancy the PM may or may not choose to fill.

basic.q: Which Article specifically deals with the Prime Minister's duty to communicate Council of Ministers' decisions to the President and furnish information as required?
basic.e: Article 78 lays out this specific duty — communicating all council decisions relating to Union administration and legislative proposals, furnishing information the President calls for, and submitting any minister's undecided-by-council matter for full council consideration if the President so requires.

basic.q: According to Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, which functionary under the Indian Constitution should actually be compared to the US President?
o: The Prime Minister, not the President of India
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
basic.e: Ambedkar stated: 'If any functionary under our constitution is to be compared with the US President, he is the Prime Minister and not the President of the Union' — highlighting that real executive power in India's parliamentary system rests with the PM, unlike the nominal, ceremonial Indian presidency.

basic.q: Which phrase did Lord Morley use to describe the British Prime Minister's position relative to the cabinet?
o: 'Inter stellas luna minores' (a moon among lesser stars)
'The captain of the ship of the state'
'The pivot around which the machinery revolves'
basic.e: Lord Morley used 'primus inter pares' ('first among equals'), also calling the PM the 'key-stone of the cabinet arch'. Other scholars used different metaphors: Harcourt called the PM 'a moon among lesser stars', Jennings called him 'a sun around which planets revolve', and Munro called him 'the captain of the ship of the state'.

basic.q: Which six people became Prime Minister of India after having previously served as Chief Minister of a state?
o: Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, V.P. Singh, P.V. Narasimha Rao, H.D. Deve Gowda, and Narendra Modi
Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi, V.P. Singh, Manmohan Singh, and Narendra Modi
Charan Singh, Chandrasekhar, I.K. Gujral, A.B. Vajpayee, Deve Gowda, and Manmohan Singh
Morarji Desai, Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi, V.P. Singh, Narasimha Rao, and Modi
basic.e: These six — Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, V.P. Singh, P.V. Narasimha Rao, H.D. Deve Gowda, and Narendra Modi — each transitioned from a state Chief Ministership to the national Prime Ministership, illustrating a recurring pathway from state to national leadership in Indian politics.

basic.q: Which committee, appointed during Jayaprakash Narayan's 'Total Revolution' movement (1974), recommended that a caretaker government should not initiate new policies or promise new projects?
basic.e: The Tarkunde Committee (1974-75), headed by Justice V.M. Tarkunde and also known as the JP Committee, recommended these specific restrictions on caretaker governments — no new policies, no new projects, no allowance/loan/salary grants, and no ministerial official functions — to prevent misuse of transitional power.

basic.q: Does the Constitution of India contain any explicit provision for a 'caretaker government'?
o: No, it is only a situational arrangement and functional necessity
Yes, it is explicitly defined under Article 75
Yes, it is explicitly defined under Article 356
No, and courts have declared the concept unconstitutional
basic.e: The Constitution has no explicit provision for a caretaker government — it is purely a situational, practical arrangement recognised by convention and judicial observation (e.g., a 1979 Calcutta High Court judgement), not a formal constitutional category.

basic.q: Which Amendment Act capped the total number of ministers (including the PM) at not exceeding 15% of the Lok Sabha's total strength?
basic.e: The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 introduced this 15% cap on council of ministers' size, and also disqualified defectors from being appointed ministers — both provisions were added to Article 75 to curb the earlier trend of unusually large 'mega' ministries formed for political accommodation.

basic.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that even after the Lok Sabha's dissolution, the council of ministers does not cease to hold office, and Article 74 is mandatory?
basic.e: The U.N.R. Rao case (1971) established that the council of ministers continues even after Lok Sabha dissolution, and that the President CANNOT exercise executive power without the council's aid and advice — doing so would violate Article 74.

basic.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that wherever the Constitution requires the President's 'satisfaction', this actually means the satisfaction of the council of ministers, not the President's personal satisfaction?
basic.e: The Shamsher Singh case (1974) clarified this crucial interpretive point — the President's 'satisfaction' referenced throughout the Constitution is legally understood as the council of ministers' collective satisfaction, reinforcing the ceremonial, advice-bound nature of the presidential office.

basic.q: In which case did the Supreme Court uphold the validity of the oath taken by Devi Lal as 'Deputy Prime Minister' in 1990, even though the Constitution does not mention this title?
basic.e: The Supreme Court upheld Devi Lal's oath as valid, ruling that describing someone as 'Deputy Prime Minister' is merely DESCRIPTIVE and doesn't confer any actual powers of the Prime Minister — such a description does not invalidate the oath so long as its SUBSTANTIVE part remains correct.

basic.q: Which three categories of ministers together make up the council of ministers?
o: Cabinet ministers, ministers of state, and deputy ministers
Cabinet ministers, junior ministers, and parliamentary secretaries
Senior ministers, state ministers, and district ministers
Cabinet ministers, deputy ministers, and shadow ministers
basic.e: The council of ministers consists of cabinet ministers, ministers of state, and deputy ministers — differing in rank, emoluments, and political importance, with the Prime Minister standing at the top of all of them as the supreme governing authority.

basic.q: Which category of ministers can either be given independent charge of a ministry/department OR be attached to work under a cabinet minister's supervision?
basic.e: Ministers of state have this dual possibility — with independent charge, they exercise the same powers as a cabinet minister over their department; when attached to a cabinet minister, they work under that minister's overall supervision and don't normally attend cabinet meetings unless specially invited.

basic.q: Which body meets frequently (usually weekly) to deliberate and take collective decisions on government business, unlike the larger council of ministers which has no such collective function?
basic.e: The Cabinet — a smaller body consisting only of cabinet ministers — meets regularly (usually weekly) as a collective decision-making body. The full council of ministers, being much larger, does not meet collectively to transact business in the same way.

basic.q: When was the term 'Cabinet' first inserted into the constitutional text, and under which Article?
o: 1978, under Article 352, by the 44th Amendment Act
1950, in the original Constitution, under Article 74
1976, under Article 74, by the 42nd Amendment Act
2003, under Article 75, by the 91st Amendment Act
basic.e: The word 'Cabinet' was inserted only in 1978, into Article 352, by the 44th Amendment Act — it did NOT appear anywhere in the Constitution's original text; even now, Article 352 only briefly defines it as 'the council consisting of the Prime Minister and other ministers of cabinet rank', without detailing its powers or functions.
